1. Problem Statement
To design a positionally adaptable orthopedic device for growing children (ages 5-7) to
accommodate up to 10% volumetric foot growth while supporting 150N of ground
reaction forces.


2. Project Background Report

2.1 Disease State & Procedure Understanding
Disease Background

Pes planus, commonly referred to as flat feet, is a common foot deformity characterized
by partial or complete loss of the medical longitudinal arch during weight-bearing.

Consists of several flexible and rigid subtypes.




Figure 1. Typical Arch vs Flat Arch secondary Pes planus [3].

Causes:

Congenital:

Infants are commonly born with flat feet and do not develop a normal arch until ages 7 to
10. This is because infants have a pad of fat that lies under the medial longitudinal arch
that protects the arch during early childhood but rapidly disappears as the child starts
walking.

However, some children might just not develop a normal arch by the time they reach
adulthood.

Acquired:

Acquired pes planus is most commonly associated with posterior tibial tendon
dysfunction, which supports the arch and provides inversion and plantarflexion of the
foot.

Dysfunction of this tendon can result from stretching, tears, or ruptures.

Likewise, patients with damage or trauma to the midfoot or hindfoot that results in
navicular, first metatarsal, calcaneal, or Lisfranc ligament complex are at an increased
risk of developing pes planus.

Other causes consist of injuries to soft tissues such as the plantar fascia or spring
ligament.

Patients who exhibit congenital ligamentous laxity due to Down syndrome, Marfan
syndrome, or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome can also present with pes planus.

Patients with rheumatoid arthritis or other degenerative or inflammatory conditions are
likewise at higher risk of pes planus.

Symptoms:

Early symptoms might include foot pain, ankle pain, and shin splints.

Over time, patients tend to develop abnormalities in their gait, deformities like bunions or
hammertoes, and even constant chronic pain.

This pain can spread upstream to the knees, hips, and lower back as well.

If left untreated, many patients develop conditions secondary to pes planus, such as
arthritis, ankle instability and strains, and other repetitive strain-based injuries.

Current Treatment Methods:

Children rarely require surgical intervention for pes planus. Foot orthotics are often the
primary treatment for foot pain resulting from pes planus in children.

However, surgery may be suggested for more severe cases of rigid pes planus, tarsal
coalitions, and progressive, symptomatic pes planus.

Limitations of Current Treatments:

The majority of treatments for pes planus are limited because most cases are
asymptomatic and developmentally normal.

Research Summary:

Molina-García, C., Banwell, G., Rodríguez-Blanque, R., Sánchez-García, J. C., Reinoso-
Cobo, A., Cortés-Martín, J., & Ramos-Petersen, L. (2023). Efficacy of Plantar Orthoses
in Paediatric Flexible Flatfoot: A Five-Year Systematic Review. Children, 10(2), 371.
https://doi.org/10.3390/children10020371

Summary: This systematic review evaluates multiple clinical trials tracking pediatric
cohorts presenting with symptomatic flexible flatfoot. The article notes that orthotics
treatment is the most commonly recommended treatment amoung pediatrics despite

lack of supporting evidence for such treatment, along with a lack of evidence supporting
the effectiveness of orthotics for this matter, indicating the presence of bias in several of
the reviewed studies in testing and validation methods.

Sharula, Zhao F, Wu T, Kang Q, Geng X, Qin H, Zhang Y, He J, Huang L, Xu J and Lu S
(2026) Treatment of pediatric flatfoot: a systematic review-based consensus and
guidelines by CPAM-LRC. Front. Pediatr. 14:1825355. doi: 10.3389/fped.2026.1825355

Summary: This multi-disciplinary clinical guideline synthesizes database trials to outline
standard care pathways for pediatric flatfoot management. The expert panel notes that
the pediatric medial longitudinal arch develops progressively during the first decade of
life, meaning that conservative treatment must avoid completely rigid immobilization to
prevent secondary muscle atrophy. The text concludes that successful conservative
interventions require designs capable of accommodating dynamic developmental
changes while simultaneously mitigating the localized pain and functional limits that
trigger clinical consultations.

Dars, S., Uden, H., Banwell, H. A., & Kumar, S. (2018). The effectiveness of non-
surgical intervention (Foot Orthoses) for paediatric flexible pes planus: A systematic
review: Update. PloS one, 13(2), e0193060.
https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0193060

Summary: This systematic review addresses the clinical efficacy and wear compliance
profiles of foot orthoses across pediatric populations. Out of 606 articles identified, 11
studies met the inclusion criteria. A diverse range of pre-fabricated and customised FOs
were utilised and effectiveness measured through a plethora of outcomes. Summarised
findings from the heterogeneous evidence base indicated that FOs may have a positive
impact across a range of outcomes including pain, foot posture, gait, function and
structural and kinetic measures. Despite these consistent positive outcomes reported in
several studies, the current evidence base lacks clarity and uniformity in terms of
diagnostic criteria, interventions delivered, and outcomes measured for paediatric
flexible pes planus.

Procedural Flow Diagram (Generated per deliverables)
1. Diagnosis: Patient aged 5-7 presents to pediatrician or podiatrist with foot fatigue,
pain, or observed gait abnormalities.
2. Assessment: Clinical evaluation of Resting Calcaneal Stance Position (RCSP) and
Medial Longitudinal Arch (MLA) collapse under load.
3. Prescription/Treatment: Recommendation of non-surgical intervention (foot orthotics)
to alleviate pain while preserving dynamic arch growth.
4. Application: Parent applies orthotic device to the child's foot daily.
5. Failure Modes in Pathway: Child refuses to wear rigid orthotic due to pain/stiffness;
device limits natural arch muscle development; device is rapidly outgrown resulting in
improper fit.

2.2 Competitive Benchmark
User Analysis:

All users of this device will fall into the three P’s: Patients, Providers, and Payers.

Each of these groups all have different needs that will have to be factored into our
design, and we should keep all stakeholders in mind when making design decisions.

First, there are multiple people to consider when thinking about the patient's needs.

Since this device is targeted at children aged 5-7 with Pes Planus, it must be not only
comfortable for the child, but easy for the child’s parent to use and put on them.

Furthermore, the device must be very durable to survive daily use from a toddler.

Overall, the patients using this will be children aged 5-7 years at risk of developing Pes
Planus, and to accommodate them best we must make an easy to use yet durable
device that will improve the child's arch.

Next, there are a wide range of providers that may recommend this device.

A pediatric podiatrist may prescribe this device to the patient at a doctor's office, a
physical therapist may suggest it during a recovery session, and a general practitioner
may refer a family to one of these professionals if the problem is presented to them.

Ideally, the doctor will only need to demonstrate how to use the device to the family and
initially set it up for the child.

This once again means the device must be easy to use, since many different
professionals may be using it, and it must work so that the doctor continues to
recommend them to families.

Overall, the needs of the provider of the device are very similar to the needs of the
patient's device: to prevent flat feet from forming and to be simple to operate.

Lastly, the payers of the device will be insurance companies and hospitals, which want
the device to make profit and be safe enough to avoid any liability.

If the device poses a significant risk to the patient, such as inducing Pes Planus instead
of preventing it, the payers will be liable for the damages that are caused.

The main priority of the payers is to get a return on their investment, meaning the device
must work well enough to sell to patients, and it must prioritize safety while doing so.

Overall, the users may have different motives for their needs, however a safe, durable
device that successfully prevents Pes Planus will make everyone happy.

2.3 Conclusion (So What?)
As synthesized from the above research and competitive benchmarking, standard rigid
orthotics present substantial limitations for pediatric patients due to the rapid volumetric
foot growth between ages 5 to 7. Traditional interventions frequently fail due to low
compliance caused by physical discomfort and the high cost of constant replacement.
Group 11’s solution presents a strong commercial and clinical opportunity by offering a
positionally adaptable, comfortable sleeve-based design that scales with the child’s
growth. This reduces pain efficiently while lowering the financial burden on parents and
payers, fulfilling a critical unmet need in pediatric podiatry.
